children: The Reserve Bank of India’s data on balance of payments for the first half of the year brings to the forefront the overall impact of the global environment on the Indian economy. It also vindicates the decision to get in the FCNR deposits and ECBs.

The trade deficit for this half of the year was higher by $18 billion at $176.1 billion. This was a result of the oil crisis which affected both imports and exports. As refinery products are an important component of the export basket, they normally tend to support the oil equation when the price of crude oil goes up. The war disruption and closure of Strait of Hormuz meant a couple of things. First there was more dependence on Russia for oil, which came at a premium to Brent. The discounts that were had after the Ukraine war had dried up. Second, the exports of refinery products to the Gulf region came down thus pressuring growth in exports.

Second, the increase in service exports was just $6.2 billion at $105 billion. Here, software is the major contributor and was affected mainly due to the global disturbances. This may change in the coming months post US elections.

Remittances, however, had increased by $10.5 billion to $77.7 billion. This is significant because it was felt that the escalation of the war could impact these remittances as the flow of labour to the Gulf area had slowed down. Also, the fact that the oil industry was in disarray could have led to lower incomes. It is possible that the western nations, which are now the major sources of remittances, have contributed to this increase, as these people typically are in higher paying jobs relative to those who work in the Gulf.

The net income from abroad also widened by $6.6 billion. All put, there has been a strain on the current account. In the past, it is the capital account which has put pressure on the balance of payments. On the capital account, first the FDI in net terms increased from $7.4 billion to $ 8.8 billion. While this is higher, ‘net FDI’ remains an issue. Outward FDI was higher by $3.4 billion at $22.1 billion. Indian companies are investing in their subsidiaries or involved in M&A activity. In a way it does show that Indian companies are progressively becoming global.

The FPI picture was disappointing at minus $10.4 billion. While it was negative last year too, it was worse this time. There are signs that there has been a major reversal this month, and hopefully with peace being more of a reality in the Gulf, or at least oil prices remaining stable, this could increase.

The ECBs and NRI deposits need to be looked at together this time. The FCNR scheme was a major success. It was based on the concept of leverage where loans were arranged to the NRIs to invest in these deposits which yielded a return of 6.75-7 per cent per annum. These loans have been arranged significantly from Indian players as is revealed by the ECB position.

The ECBs ‘by India’ were at an all-time high of $51.4 billion. This was only $3.4 billion for the first quarter which does correlate the outflow with the FCNR scheme. It would appear that a part of these loans would have been used for leveraging the FCNR scheme. There would also be lending made by Indian companies to other overseas companies on which information is not provided separately.

The balance of payments was finally in positive territory and stood at $66.8 billion. This was largely due to the combo of FCNR and ECBs. This has also contributed to rupee stability. The country will have to arrange for the redemptions which start after three years, making forex management a 365-day affair.
The writer is Chief Economist, Bank of Baroda.

title: FCNR flows shore up first quarter BoP
